We will show that if 
  • h = 2^r with r = 0 (that is, h = 1), then every natural number k works,
  • but if r ≥ 1 (so h ≥ 2) then one may find an odd number m > 1 and a natural number n with
sentence-category-reason: Announces the intention to prove a result with case distinctions; outlines what will be shown.

sentence: (1) k divides m^h – 1 and (2) m divides n^((m^h–1)/k) + 1
sentence-category-reason: Restates the exact divisibility conditions from the problem.

(In other words, writing
   k = 2^a · k₀ with k₀ odd, a necessary and sufficient condition is that a ≥ r + 2.
sentence-category-reason: Gives the explicit necessary and sufficient condition answering the problem.

sentence: A reformulation using the 2–adic valuation
sentence-category-reason: Introduces the intended approach (a reformulation using 2-adic valuation).

sentence: Suppose h = 2^r with r a nonnegative integer.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the given assumption about h.

sentence:
The stated condition is that there exist an odd m > 1 and a natural number n for which
  (1) k | (m^h – 1)
and
  (2) m | (n^d + 1), where d = (m^h – 1)/k.
sentence-category-reason: Reformulates the condition and introduces the notation d = (m^h−1)/k.

sentence: It turns out that a necessary (and eventually sufficient) condition is that the “exponent” d is odd.
sentence-category-reason: States a necessary (and planned sufficient) condition about the exponent d being odd.

sentence: (In (2) one must be able to find some n with n^d ≡ –1 mod m, and a standard fact about kth–power residues shows that (under mild hypotheses) a necessary and sufficient condition is that d be odd.
sentence-category-reason: Justifies the necessity/sufficiency of d being odd by appealing to a standard residues fact.

sentence:
Thus we must have
  (m^h – 1)/k odd.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces that (m^h−1)/k must be odd.

sentence:
Write the prime factorization of m^h – 1 as
  m^h – 1 = 2^A · O   (with O odd).
sentence-category-reason: Introduces a factorization and new notation (A and O).

sentence:
Then (m^h – 1)/k is odd if and only if k contains exactly the entire power of 2 that appears in m^h – 1; that is, if and only if
  v₂(k) = A.
sentence-category-reason: Derives an equivalence condition in terms of v2(k) and A.

sentence: (Here v₂(x) denotes the exponent of 2 in x.
sentence-category-reason: Defines the notation v2(x) as the exponent of 2 in x.

sentence:
Now, for an odd m and h = 2^r (with r ≥ 1) one may use the “Lifting‐the–Exponent Lemma” to show that
  v₂(m^h – 1) = v₂(m – 1) + v₂(m + 1) + r – 1.
sentence-category-reason: Applies LTE to derive a valuation identity; theoretical deduction.

sentence: But note that for any odd number m the two even numbers m – 1 and m + 1 are consecutive even numbers so that one of them is divisible by 2 exactly while the other is divisible by at least 4.
sentence-category-reason: Observes properties of m−1 and m+1 regarding powers of 2.

sentence: (More precisely, if m ≡ 1 mod 4 then v₂(m – 1) ≥ 2 while v₂(m + 1) = 1, and if m ≡ 3 mod 4 then v₂(m – 1) = 1 while v₂(m + 1) ≥ 2.
sentence-category-reason: Gives the precise valuations in the two congruence classes of m mod 4.

sentence:
) In either case one sees that
  v₂(m^h – 1) = r + s  with some integer s ≥ 2.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes the general form v2(m^h−1) = r + s with s ≥ 2 from prior observations.

sentence:
Thus if m and h = 2^r (r ≥ 1) are given then necessarily
  v₂(k) = r + s with some s ≥ 2.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces a necessary condition on v2(k) from prior results; logical inference without calculation.

sentence:
That is, if one writes
  k = 2^a · k₀  (with k₀ odd),
then necessarily for the existence of m (and n) the exponent a must satisfy
  a = r + s with s ≥ 2, that is, a ≥ r + 2.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the necessary condition on the exponent a in k=2^a·k0; deduction without computation.
Section header indicating a transition to a new step.

sentence: Verifying sufficiency
sentence-category-reason: Introduces the act of verifying sufficiency; per guidelines such verification cues are categorized as Verify.

sentence:
One may show that conversely, if we are given a natural number k whose 2–part satisfies
  v₂(k) = a with a ≥ r + 2,
then one may “build” an odd m > 1 (and then an n in ℕ) so that
  m^h – 1 is divisible by k
and such that the quotient d = (m^h – 1)/k is odd; the latter fact then guarantees that an n with n^d ≡ –1 mod m exists.
sentence-category-reason: Conceptually explains the sufficiency claim and why odd d guarantees existence of n.

sentence: For example, one way to proceed is as follows.
sentence-category-reason: Announces a specific approach to construct m and n.

sentence:
Write
  k = 2^(r+s) · k₀ with s ≥ 2 and k₀ odd.
sentence-category-reason: Carries out a concrete step by expressing k in the required form.

sentence:
Then choose an odd number m so that
  v₂(m – 1) = s  and  v₂(m + 1) = 1
(which is possible since the two possibilities for m mod 4 are exactly “m ≡ 1 mod 4” and “m ≡ 3 mod 4”).
sentence-category-reason: Selects m with specified 2-adic properties and justifies possibility; constructive action.

sentence:
Then
  v₂(m^h – 1) = s + 1 + r – 1 = r + s,
so that 2^(r+s) exactly divides m^h – 1.
sentence-category-reason: Performs a concrete calculation of v2(m^h−1) and its divisibility by a power of 2.

sentence: With some extra work one may adjust m (using, say, the Chinese remainder theorem on the odd part) so that the odd factor of m^h – 1 is a multiple of k₀.
sentence-category-reason: Outlines the next adjustment using CRT to handle the odd part; planning a step.

sentence: In this way one obtains m for which k divides m^h – 1 and the quotient (m^h – 1)/k is odd, so that (2) is soluble in n.
sentence-category-reason: Confirms the constructed m satisfies the divisibility and that condition (2) is solvable; evaluative conclusion.

sentence: A separate (and much easier) argument shows that when h = 1 (that is, r = 0) one may take m equal to 1+k (so that m–1 = k) and then (m–1)/k = 1 is odd.
sentence-category-reason: Provides a concrete construction for h=1 and computes the resulting quotient.

sentence: Hence in that case every k works.
sentence-category-reason: States the resulting conclusion for the h=1 case.

sentence: An acceptable answer is therefore: • If h = 2^r with r = 0 (so h = 1), then every natural number k works.
sentence-category-reason: Presents part of the final answer for r=0 explicitly.

sentence:
• If h = 2^r with r ≥ 1 then there exist an odd natural number m > 1 and a natural number n satisfying
  k | m^h – 1 and m | n^((m^h–1)/k) + 1
if and only if when writing k = 2^a · k₀ (with k₀ odd) one has
  a ≥ r + 2.
sentence-category-reason: States the main if-and-only-if condition for r≥1 as the answer.

sentence: Equivalently, k must be divisible by 2^(r+2).
sentence-category-reason: Gives an equivalent concise statement of the final condition.

sentence: Any answer equivalent to the above is correct.

sentence:
For h = 2^r, the answer is as follows:
 – When h = 1 (that is, r = 0), every natural number k has the property.
sentence-category-reason: States the result for the case h=1 directly as part of the final solution.

sentence:
– When h = 2^r with r ≥ 1, write k = 2^a · k₀ with k₀ odd; then there exist an odd m > 1 and n ∈ ℕ satisfying
  k | m^(2^r) – 1 and m | n^((m^(2^r) – 1)/k) + 1
if and only if a ≥ r + 2 (i.e. 2^(r+2) divides k).
sentence-category-reason: Gives the necessary and sufficient condition on k (a ≥ r+2) for r ≥ 1, which is the main final result.
